# Citation Link Prediction

You inherit a weak baseline on a link prediction problem. Make it as strong as you can.

## Hard Constraints

- Modify only the contents of `methods/main/`.
- Keep the command line contract exactly:
  `python solve.py --data-dir <DATA> --out <OUT.pt> [--split {val,test}]`
  The grader runs the default `--split test`. `selfcheck.py` runs `--split val`
  and scores the visible validation split with the same metric.
- The submission is copied into a clean environment and run **once** on data you
  have not seen. Anything you memorise about the visible data will not transfer.
- No network access.
- Do not attempt to read files outside `<DATA>` and your own `methods/main/`.

## What You Have

`<DATA>/dataset.pt` is a dict whose contents depend on the task:

  - `x` `[N, F]` float node features
  - `edge_index` `[2, E]` long, the graph used for message passing
  - `num_nodes` int
  - `train_edges` `[2, T]`, `train_neg` `[2, T]` (positive and negative pairs)
  - `val_edges` `[2, V]`; `val_neg` is `[2, V']` (a flat pool), or `[V, K, 2]`
    when every validation positive has its own K negatives (MRR tasks)
  - `--split val` must score, in this order: `cat([val_edges, val_neg], dim=1)`
    for a flat pool; for grouped negatives, per positive `i`, the pair
    `val_edges[:, i]` followed by its K pairs `val_neg[i]`
  - **the test pairs are not here.** At scoring time the grader adds
    `<DATA>/test_inputs.pt` = `{"candidates": [2, C] long}`, a shuffled mix of
    positive and negative pairs. You must score every row; you are not told which
    is which.

`methods/main/solve.py` is a working but weak baseline. Rewrite it entirely if you
want; only the command line contract and the output keys are fixed.

## What You Submit

The complete `methods/main/` directory.

## How It Is Judged

Your program is re-run from scratch. It must write a dict to `--out`:

  `{"scores": <[C] float>}` — one score per column of
  `<DATA>/test_inputs.pt["candidates"]` (`[2, C]`), in the same order. Higher means more
  likely to be a true edge.

Metric: **MRR, higher is better.** Scored with the official
benchmark evaluator on held-out data.
